sketches.title: Last Screening Standing
sketches.premise: You get the same ordinary noun as the other player. Turn it into a film title and a tagline for a tiny event; the Judge rewards the biggest leap from the noun while the title still sounds like a film and the tagline still sells that exact film. Then each of you calls which rival entry best fits the card's hidden fact.
sketches.criterion: The title and tagline must together remain a coherent film-and-event pitch built around the card's noun.
sketches.move_shape: Write `Title — tagline` in one line; for `spoon`: `SPOON — One small utensil, one very large betrayal.`

sketches.title: Wrong Trailer
sketches.premise: Both players receive one everyday noun and pitch a film title plus a tagline for a small event, but the event has a secret trailer fact such as its setting, audience, or practical problem. Stretch the noun as far as possible without making the pitch contradict that fact; then call which pitch respected the hidden trailer. The House's fact is checked after the call.
sketches.criterion: Every detail must remain compatible with the card's hidden, checkable trailer fact.
sketches.move_shape: Write `Title — tagline`; for `ladder`: `LADDER TO NOWHERE — A rooftop romance for an audience that hates heights.`

sketches.title: Double-Feature Damage
sketches.premise: A card gives you two plain nouns. Combine them into a film title and a tagline for a small event, making the combination feel unexpectedly ambitious rather than merely accurate. The Judge scores the distance between the nouns and the pitch, provided both nouns still matter; then players call which entry better preserves the card's real connection.
sketches.criterion: Both nouns must remain meaningfully present in one coherent film-and-event pitch.
sketches.move_shape: Write `Title — tagline`; for `shoe / moon`: `MOONSHOE — A midnight dance class for people who have stopped trusting gravity.`

sketches.title: Tagline Under Oath
sketches.premise: You receive a familiar noun and write a film title and tagline for a small event. The title may go gloriously sideways, but the tagline must make one concrete claim that remains true of the noun; the farther the title travels while that claim holds, the more it scores. Then call which rival tagline is the real one supplied by the House.
sketches.criterion: The tagline must make a true, checkable claim about the card's noun, while title and tagline still form one pitch.
sketches.move_shape: Write `Title — tagline`; for `window`: `WINDOWS FOR THE DAMNED — Glass can break, but it cannot be argued with.`

sketches.title: Tiny Festival, Big Lie
sketches.premise: Both players get the same everyday noun and invent a film title and event tagline that confidently misclassify it: make it sound like a thriller, romance, or documentary while preserving one plain fact about the noun. A bland fact earns almost nothing; a wild premise earns points only while its factual anchor survives. Players then call which entry's anchor is the House's real one.
sketches.criterion: The pitch may change the noun's genre and status, but it must preserve one stated, checkable fact about it.
sketches.move_shape: Write `Title — tagline`, with the preserved fact embedded; for `chair`: `THE CHAIR KNOWS — It has four legs and absolutely no patience.`

sketches.title: Poster Child
sketches.premise: A card supplies two ordinary nouns that share a real relationship. Make a film title and tagline for a small event that turns that relationship into a sharp, adult poster line without spelling it out. The Judge rewards the most surprising implication that still keeps the relationship intact; then players call which poster captured the House's actual relationship.
sketches.criterion: The title and tagline must preserve the card's real relationship between both nouns without naming it so plainly that the pitch becomes dull.
sketches.move_shape: Write `Title — tagline`; for `lock / key`: `ACCESS DENIED — Every secret thinks it is the important one.`
